claims.title: Asymmetric authorization on certificate routes (GET vs PUT/DELETE)
claims.impact: GET allows unauthorized read; PUT/DELETE deny unauthorized write. Violates principle of uniform access control. Measured blind spot for scanners (asymmetric authorization is harder to detect than uniform failures).
claims.evidence: GET handler: no authorization check. PUT handler (line 942): checks CertificatePermission(certificate_id).can(). DELETE handler (line 1154): checks permission. All handle the same resource (certificate).

claims.title: Dependabot auto-merge enabled without human review (supply chain drift risk)
claims.impact: One malicious transitive dependency can be auto-merged and deployed. No human review gates the change. If Dependabot is compromised (e.g., to inject false updates), malicious code auto-deploys.
claims.evidence: Workflow auto-merges dependabot PRs for patch and minor version updates without requiring human approval.

claims.title: PII Exposure via Sentry Integration
claims.impact: Sentry is configured with send_default_pii=True, which automatically sends personally identifiable information (user IDs, IP addresses, usernames) to Sentry servers. This violates privacy policies and GDPR.
claims.evidence: send_default_pii=True,

claims.title: Broken object-level authorization (BOLA) on GET /certificates/{id}
claims.impact: Any authenticated user can enumerate and read all certificates by ID, including private keys. Violates API1:2023 (broken object-level authorization). Asymmetric authorization: write operations are protected, read is not.
claims.evidence: GET handler retrieves certificate via service.get(certificate_id) with no authorization check. PUT/DELETE/POST correctly enforce CertificatePermission. GET does not.

claims.title: Weak JWT Signature Algorithm Default
claims.impact: JWT tokens use HS256 (HMAC with shared secret) as default. If LEMUR_TOKEN_SECRET is compromised, attackers can forge valid tokens and impersonate any user.
claims.evidence: signing_alg = current_app.config.get('LEMUR_TOKEN_ALGORITHMS', ['HS256'])[0]

claims.title: Base images use moving tags instead of SHA256 digests (reproducibility broken)
claims.impact: Tags are mutable; image digest can change at any time. Reproducibility broken: same docker-compose.yml can pull different images on different runs. Supply chain attack: if image is compromised on registry, all builds after compromise are affected.
claims.evidence: image: postgres:13.1-alpine (not pinned by digest); image: redis:alpine3.12 (moving tag); FROM python:3.8

claims.title: Shared JWT Token Secret Across All API Keys
claims.impact: All API key JWTs use the same server secret; if compromised, all tokens are compromised
claims.evidence: Lines 88-91: All tokens signed with single LEMUR_TOKEN_SECRET from config

claims.title: Uncontrolled Exception Message Disclosure
claims.impact: Custom exception messages are returned to clients, potentially leaking implementation details
claims.evidence: Line 541: return dict(message=str(e)), 403 - UnauthorizedError exception details returned to client

claims.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in OpenID Connect Validation
claims.impact: Server-Side Request Forgery - Can make requests to internal services/metadata endpoints
claims.evidence:
Code: r = requests.get(jwks_url)
Fetches JWKS from user-provided or config-specified URL without validating it. jwks_url comes from OpenID Connect provider configuration and could be manipulated to access internal services.

claims.title: Outdated Redis image alpine3.12 in docker-compose (EOL, no patches)
claims.impact: Alpine 3.12 reached EOL 2022-05-23. No security patches available. Redis and underlying packages have unpatched CVEs.
claims.evidence: image: 'redis:alpine3.12'

claims.title: Missing CSRF Protection Configuration
claims.impact: The application does not show explicit CSRF protection configuration. Without CSRF tokens, state parameters, or SameSite cookie attributes properly configured, attackers could potentially perform cross-site request forgery attacks on state-changing operations (certificate issuance, user creation, etc.) if users are authenticated in other browser tabs.
claims.evidence: The Flask-CORS integration at lines 179-191 configures CORS but there is no visible CSRF token validation or protection middleware configured in the factory.

claims.title: Insufficient Input Validation for Sorting Parameters
claims.impact: Although get_model_column() validates field names, request parameters are not pre-validated. Attackers could exploit edge cases or timing issues.
claims.evidence: def sort(query, model, field, direction): column = get_model_column(model, underscore(field))

claims.title: Permissive CORS Configuration
claims.impact: CORS is configured with wildcard origin ('*'), allowing any website to make API requests. This enables cross-site request forgery (CSRF), data exfiltration, and unauthorized API access from malicious sites.
claims.evidence: app.config['CORS_ORIGINS'] = '*'

claims.title: XXE (XML External Entity) Vulnerability in Verisign Plugin
claims.impact: An attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack on Verisign API responses or compromising the Verisign API could inject malicious XML to read local files, cause denial of service, or perform SSRF attacks.
claims.evidence: The xmltodict.parse(content) function at line 168 is called without disabling XML entity expansion. The function uses handle_response() to parse XML from the Verisign API without any XXE protections enabled.

claims.title: GitHub Actions unpinned to commit SHA (supply chain attack surface)
claims.impact: Mutable version tags (@v6, @release/v1) can be retargeted to malicious commits. An attacker compromising GitHub or action maintainers can inject code that runs with GITHUB_TOKEN during CI/CD. Code executes with repository access and deployment permissions.
claims.evidence: uses: actions/checkout@v6 (not pinned to @sha256:...); uses: actions/setup-python@v6; uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1

claims.title: Conditional HTTPS Certificate Verification Bypass
claims.impact: HTTPS certificate verification can be disabled via the verify_cert parameter. This enables man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks when verify_cert=False, allowing interception of OAuth tokens and sensitive data.
claims.evidence: r = requests.post(access_token_url, headers=headers, params=params, verify=verify_cert)

claims.title: Outdated SQLAlchemy dependency with unpatched vulnerabilities
claims.impact: SQLAlchemy 1.3.24 may contain unpatched SQL injection vulnerabilities (CWE-89) or other database-layer defects discovered after its release. Specific CVEs would depend on which vulnerabilities have been published for this version.
claims.evidence: requirements.txt line 331: sqlalchemy==1.3.24. SQLAlchemy 1.3 series reached end-of-life in April 2023. Current stable series is 2.0+. Version 1.3.24 is from 2023 and predates security advisories fixed in later 1.3.x releases and all of 2.0.x.

claims.title: Weak Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoint
claims.impact: The login endpoint has a rate limit of 10 requests per 5 minutes (2 requests per minute). This allows brute-force attacks to proceed at a rate of 120 attempts per hour, which is relatively easy to exploit with distributed attackers or automated tools.
claims.evidence: The @limiter.limit('10/5minute') decorator on the Login class's post() method at line ~188 shows weak rate limiting configured for the authentication endpoint. No rate limiting is visible on API endpoints that may be subject to enumeration or brute-force attacks.

claims.title: Unsafe exec() in configuration file loading allows arbitrary code execution
claims.impact: Complete system compromise via arbitrary code execution if attacker controls config source.
claims.evidence: exec() loads Python configuration without validation: exec(compile(config_file.read(), file_path, 'exec'), d.__dict__). Config sources: (1) CLI arg, (2) LEMUR_CONF env var, (3) ~/.lemur/lemur.conf.py, (4) default.conf.py.

claims.title: No SBOM or provenance attestation attached to PyPI releases
claims.impact: Consumers cannot verify which dependencies are in the wheel (supply-chain visibility). Cannot verify build was authorized by source (SLSA Build L1 missing). Post-incident forensics impossible without re-downloading and analyzing offline.
claims.evidence: Release workflow builds wheel and publishes to PyPI. No SBOM generation, no provenance attestation attached to GitHub release or PyPI package.

claims.title: Unchecked Config Callable Execution
claims.impact: Denial of Service / Application Crash - TypeError if config value is None
claims.evidence:
Code: message, code = current_app.config.get("CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION")(data)
Calls config value as function without checking if it's None first. If configuration key is not set, get() returns None, causing TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable.

claims.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via Configuration File
claims.impact: Configuration files are executed via exec() with compile(). An attacker who can control the config file path or contents can execute arbitrary Python code with the privileges of the Lemur application.
claims.evidence: exec(compile(config_file.read(), file_path, 'exec'), d.__dict__)

claims.title: Flask v2.3.3 past end-of-support (2025-04-28)
claims.impact: No security patches available. Any CVE in Flask 2.3 exploitable with no upstream fix.

claims.title: Dockerfile uses end-of-life Python 3.8 base image with known vulnerabilities
claims.impact: Python 3.8 reached end-of-life on 2024-10-07. No security patches available. Inherits all CVEs from unmaintained Python runtime.
claims.evidence: FROM python:3.8

claims.title: Outdated pip version 20.0.2 pinned (6+ years old, known CVEs)
claims.impact: pip 20.0.2 (2020) contains multiple unpatched CVEs in dependency resolution and package verification (CVE-2020-15522, CVE-2021-3572). Weakens supply chain: malicious packages can be injected.
claims.evidence: RUN pip install pip==20.0.2

claims.title: File Handle Resource Leak in Logging
claims.impact: A file is opened without a context manager or explicit close(). The handle is never released, causing a resource leak. Over time, file descriptor exhaustion can cause service failure.
claims.evidence: handler = StreamHandler(open(logfile, 'a'))

claims.title: Incorrect bandit scan path in pre-commit configuration
claims.impact: Bandit scans non-existent 'consoleme' directory, not 'lemur/'. Hook succeeds silently; no vulnerabilities detected.
claims.evidence: args: ['--ini', 'tox.ini', '-r', 'consoleme'] (but consoleme dir does not exist)

claims.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in User Information Retrieval
claims.impact: Server-Side Request Forgery - Can make requests to internal services
claims.evidence:
Code: r = requests.get(user_api_url, params=user_params, headers=headers)
Fetches user info from URL without validation. user_api_url is configuration-driven and could be manipulated to probe internal network or services.

claims.title: Certificate upload endpoint lacks authorization gate present in creation endpoint
claims.impact: BFLA - Authenticated user can upload certificates to authorities they lack permission for, bypassing authority-level access controls.
claims.evidence:
Two endpoints create Certificates with asymmetric authorization:

CertificatesList (POST /certificates): checks AuthorityPermission(data['authority'].id, roles).can()

CertificatesUpload (POST /certificates/upload): no AuthorityPermission check, calls service.upload(**data) directly

Both endpoints process 'authority' parameter; upload bypasses permission check.

claims.title: Timezone-Unsafe Timestamp Conversion
claims.impact: datetime.fromtimestamp() without timezone information assumes local timezone. In distributed systems or when configuration changes, this causes inconsistent token expiry validation.
claims.evidence: expired_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(access_key.issued_at) + timedelta(days=access_key.ttl)

claims.title: Debug Mode Exception Exposure
claims.impact: When DEBUG=True, detailed exception information is exposed to clients. This reveals internal system details, file paths, and implementation specifics useful for attackers.
claims.evidence: if current_app.config.get('DEBUG', False): raise

claims.title: Potential Insecure Random Token Generation
claims.impact: If random number generation for tokens uses Python's random module instead of secrets module, tokens could be predictable.
claims.evidence: Need to verify token generation uses secrets.token_urlsafe() or similar cryptographically secure functions

claims.title: Debug Mode Exposes Encrypted Sensitive Data
claims.impact: When DEBUG mode is enabled, encrypted sensitive values are logged to the application log, potentially exposing encrypted credentials
claims.evidence: Line 127: current_app.logger.error(f"Error decrypting token: {value}") logs the encrypted value when DEBUG=True

claims.title: Weak Authorization Check for Certificate Creation
claims.impact: Authorization depends on a simple boolean flag is_admin_or_global_cert_issuer which may not properly enforce domain restrictions
claims.evidence: Lines 538-539: Authorization check uses 'is_admin_or_global_cert_issuer' flag without granular per-domain validation

claims.title: Index Out of Bounds Error in Database Filter Helper
claims.impact: Denial of Service - Unhandled IndexError in database operations
claims.evidence:
Code: column = get_model_column(model, underscore(terms[0])); return query.filter(column.ilike(f"%{terms[1]}%"))
Accesses terms[1] without validating that split() produced sufficient parts. Called from certificate rendering with user-supplied filter parameters.

claims.title: Production container runs as root (privilege escalation risk)
claims.file: Dockerfile (no explicit USER declaration; defaults to root)
claims.impact: Container runs as root. Any RCE/command injection allows full container escape. Attacker gains access to filesystem, networks, mounted volumes.
claims.evidence: No 'USER lemur' or 'USER <uid>' directive in Dockerfile

claims.title: Unchecked Config Callable Execution - Export Key Validation
claims.impact: Denial of Service - TypeError if config value is None
claims.evidence:
Code: message, code = current_app.config.get("CERTIFICATE_EXPORT_KEY_REQUEST_VALIDATION")(cert, g.current_user)
Same pattern as F-003. No null check before calling retrieved function.

claims.title: Sentry configured to export PII in error tracking
claims.impact: Users' PII (email, username, IP, full request data) is transmitted to Sentry whenever an error occurs and Sentry is configured. This violates privacy principles of data minimization and can violate regulations like GDPR depending on data processing agreements with Sentry.
claims.evidence: sentry_sdk.init(..., send_default_pii=True, ...) in configure_extensions() function at line 174. This flag causes Sentry to automatically capture personally identifiable information (email addresses, usernames, IP addresses, HTTP request details) and transmit them to Sentry's remote servers without explicit user consent or data minimization.

claims.title: CORS configured with wildcard origin by default
claims.impact: Any website the user visits can make authenticated requests to the Lemur API if the user is logged in. This enables cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks where a malicious site can perform actions on behalf of the authenticated user (create certificates, modify configurations, revoke certificates, etc.).
claims.evidence: In configure_extensions() at line 182: if "CORS_ORIGINS" not in app.config: app.config["CORS_ORIGINS"] = "*". This sets CORS Allow-Origin to "*" (wildcard) if no explicit configuration is provided, which permits any web origin to make cross-origin requests to the Lemur API.

claims.title: Insecure CORS Configuration with Wildcard Origin
claims.impact: If CORS is enabled and CORS_ORIGINS is not explicitly configured, the application allows cross-origin requests from ANY origin (*). This allows any website to make authenticated API requests on behalf of users, potentially leading to unauthorized certificate issuance, access to sensitive certificate data, or other API abuse.
claims.evidence: Lines 181-184 show that if CORS is enabled and CORS_ORIGINS is not configured, it defaults to '*'. This is an insecure default that allows unrestricted cross-origin access.

claims.title: Evidence of Prior Cleartext Password Storage Vulnerability
claims.impact: The code references GHSA-q437-g7fv-2jvv, a vulnerability where user passwords were stored in cleartext in the database due to a missing before_update listener. While the migration function exists to detect and re-hash affected passwords, this indicates a past security failure in the authentication system.
claims.evidence: The rehash_passwords() function at lines 377-408 is designed to detect and fix cleartext passwords in the database. The function checks for passwords that don't start with bcrypt prefix ($2), indicating they were stored in plaintext due to a missing listener.

claims.title: Pre-commit config uses deprecated git:// protocol (unencrypted)
claims.impact: git:// protocol is unauthenticated and unencrypted. MITM attacker can inject malicious pre-commit hooks. Hooks execute with developer permissions during commit.
claims.evidence: repo: git://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks (port 9418, unencrypted)

claims.title: Missing input validation on filter parameter causes IndexError
claims.impact: Denial of Service on certificate lookup endpoint. Error leaks internal details aiding reconnaissance.
claims.evidence: Code splits filter without validation: common_name = args['filter'].split(';')[1]. No try/catch. If format is invalid (missing semicolon), raises IndexError. Test: GET /certificates/valid?filter=test returns 500.

claims.evidence: payload = jwt.decode(encoded_jwt, secret, algorithms=algorithms, options={'verify_sub': False})

claims.title: Unverified LDAP Security Configuration
claims.impact: LDAP configuration requires verification that it uses proper encryption (StartTLS or SSL on port 636). Without encryption, credentials are transmitted in cleartext.
claims.evidence: LDAP authentication module may not enforce secure connection settings

claims.title: SQLAlchemy v1.3.24 past end-of-support (since 2021-05-16)
claims.impact: No patches available since 2021. ORM, connection pooling, query compilation unsupported.
claims.evidence: sqlalchemy==1.3.24 (EOL 2021-05-16, 64 months past)

claims.title: Unchecked Config Callable Execution - Update Validation
claims.impact: Denial of Service - TypeError if config value is None
claims.evidence:
Code: message, code = current_app.config.get("CERTIFICATE_UPDATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION")(data, cert)
Pattern repeated multiple times (lines 952, 1107, 1280, etc). No validation that config callback exists.

claims.title: Hardcoded PostgreSQL credentials in docker-compose (plaintext exposure)
claims.impact: Credentials stored in version control or .env file visible to anyone with repository access or container inspect permissions.
claims.evidence: env_file: - pgsql-env (referenced) — file not committed; but if .env pattern, would be: POSTGRES_USER: lemur, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: lemur

claims.title: Potential Privilege Escalation via Config File Execution
claims.impact: The application executes Python code from configuration files using exec(). If an attacker can write to the default config file location (~/.lemur/lemur.conf.py) or manipulate the config file path via race conditions, they could execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Lemur process.
claims.evidence: Lines 103-106 show exec(compile(config_file.read(), file_path, 'exec'), d.__dict__) which executes arbitrary Python code from the config file. The comment 'nosec: config file safe' suppresses security warnings but doesn't eliminate the risk.

claims.title: Unsafe curl | bash pattern in Dockerfile (arbitrary code execution)
claims.impact: Piping curl to bash executes arbitrary remote code with root privileges. MITM attacker or compromised server can inject malicious code.
claims.evidence: RUN curl -sL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_18.x | bash -

claims.title: TLS certificate verification can be disabled via configuration in OAuth2 flow
claims.impact: An attacker on the network between Lemur and the OAuth2 provider can intercept the token exchange, capturing the authorization code and access tokens. This allows the attacker to impersonate any user authenticating via OAuth2.
claims.evidence: Line 594 reads `verify_cert = current_app.config.get("OAUTH2_VERIFY_CERT")`. This value is passed directly to `exchange_for_access_token()` on line 604, which uses it in `requests.post(verify=verify_cert)` on lines 80 and 84. If OAUTH2_VERIFY_CERT is set to False, SSL/TLS certificate verification is disabled, allowing MITM attacks on the OAuth2 token exchange.

claims.title: Index Out of Bounds Error in Certificate Query Filter
claims.impact: Denial of Service - Unhandled IndexError causes 500 error
claims.evidence:
Code: common_name = args.pop("filter").split(";")[1]
Accesses index [1] without checking if split() returned enough elements. If filter parameter is provided without semicolon or with insufficient parts, raises IndexError.

claims.title: CORS Misconfiguration - Wildcard Origin with Credentials
claims.impact: When CORS is enabled, it defaults to accepting requests from any origin (*) with credentials=True, allowing cross-origin attacks to steal user data
claims.evidence: Lines 179-190: CORS defaults to '*' origins with supports_credentials=True when enabled

claims.title: JWKS endpoint fetched without certificate pinning or signature verification
claims.impact: An attacker on the network can intercept the JWKS fetch and return forged public keys. This allows the attacker to create valid-looking JWT tokens signed with their own private key that Lemur will accept as genuine user tokens, leading to authentication bypass and account takeover.
claims.evidence: Line 121 makes a GET request to `jwks_url` using `requests.get()` with no parameters to pin certificates or verify the response. The response is parsed as JSON and the public keys are extracted. An attacker who can perform a MITM attack on this request could return a malicious JWKS containing attacker-controlled public keys, allowing them to forge valid JWT tokens that would be accepted by the validation logic.

claims.title: Dynamic role creation from identity provider groups allows privilege escalation
claims.impact: An attacker who can control their group membership at the identity provider (e.g., by compromising their own IdP user profile, or if the IdP allows self-service group creation) can create a role with a name similar to built-in roles, gaining elevated privileges within Lemur.
claims.evidence: Lines 237-258 show that for each group returned by the identity provider in the user profile, if the group name matches the naming conventions (prefix and suffix), a role is automatically created and assigned to the user. The code attempts to protect built-in roles (line 238) by checking for exact strings 'admin', 'operator', 'read-only'. However, a user could request membership in a group named 'admin_team' or '000admin' (depending on prefix/suffix configuration) and bypass this protection.

claims.title: Index Out of Bounds Error in Certificate Render Function
claims.impact: Denial of Service - Unhandled IndexError causes 500 error
claims.evidence:
Code: term = f"%{terms[1]}%"
Accesses index [1] without checking if split(";") returned enough elements. Missing bounds validation allows malformed filter parameters to crash the application.

advisories_to_match.summary: Lemur: Any user can revoke arbitrary certificates at the CA by uploading a duplicate record and revoking it
advisories_to_match.description:
## Summary

Repo under test: https://github.com/Netflix/lemur

`PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke` authorizes the caller against the *Lemur database row* (creator == current user, or `CertificatePermission` over the row's roles) rather than the underlying CA-side certificate identity. Separately, `POST /api/1/certificates/upload` lets any user passing `StrictRolePermission` create a new `Certificate` row while freely supplying `body`, `authority` (resolved by id/name with no `AuthorityPermission` check) and `external_id`; there is no uniqueness constraint on `body`, `serial`, or `external_id`.

An attacker can therefore read a target certificate's public `body`, `authority.id`, and `external_id` via `GET /certificates/<id>`, upload a duplicate row, and revoke that duplicate. The creator-bypass skips `CertificatePermission`, the empty-endpoints check passes because the duplicate has none, and `service.revoke()` then revokes at the CA using the attacker-supplied `body` (ACME) or `external_id` (DigiCert/Entrust/Google CA/CFSSL) under the authority's stored CA credentials — revoking the real production certificate.

## Affected route

`POST /api/1/certificates/upload` → `PUT /api/1/c
